modules.title: How the Web Works & HTTP
modules.tagline: The request/response cycle, DNS and TLS, and HTTP semantics you can reason about — not memorize.
objectives: Trace a URL from DNS resolution through TCP and the TLS handshake to a rendered page, naming each hop.
Choose the correct HTTP method and status code for any read or write, and justify it from HTTP semantics.
Explain safety, idempotency, statelessness, and caching, and predict how each affects retries and correctness.
Read a raw HTTP message and reason about the role of each header.

lessons.title: The request / response cycle, in depth
glossary: The client (browser, app) initiates a request; the server listens and returns a response. Roles, not machines — a server can itself be a client to another server.
Domain Name System — a distributed, cached lookup that resolves a hostname like api.example.com to an IP address.
Transmission Control Protocol — a reliable, ordered byte stream established via a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK).
Transport Layer Security — encrypts the TCP stream and authenticates the server via a certificate; the basis of HTTPS.
The time for a packet to reach the server and a reply to return; latency is dominated by the number of round trips.
Key/value metadata attached to a request or response (Host, Content-Type, Authorization).
The actual bytes carried by a message — form data or JSON going up, HTML or JSON coming down.

blocks.html: Every app you will ever build rides on one exchange repeated billions of times a day: a client sends a request, a server returns a response. Understand this exchange precisely — every hop, every cost — and the network stops being magic and becomes something you can debug.

blocks.title: What actually happens when you press Enter on https://app.example.com
steps: URL parse
The browser splits the URL into scheme (https), host (app.example.com), port (implicitly 443), path, and query string.
DNS lookup
It resolves the host to an IP (e.g. 93.184.216.34), checking the OS and browser caches before asking a resolver — often 0 round trips when cached, 1+ when not.
TCP handshake
It opens a connection to that IP on port 443 with a three-way handshake — one round trip before any data.
TLS handshake
For https it negotiates keys and verifies the server's certificate — one more round trip on TLS 1.3, two on older versions.
HTTP request
Only now does it send the request line, headers, and optional body over the encrypted channel.
Server work
The server routes the request, runs your code, perhaps queries a database, and assembles a response.
Response + render
Back comes a status line, headers, and a body. The browser parses HTML into the DOM and fetches CSS, JS, and images — each its own request.

blocks.html: A raw HTTP request is just text with a strict shape: a request line, then headers, a blank line, then an optional body. Here is what the browser sends and gets back:

blocks.code:
GET /api/bookings?date=2026-08-01 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGci...
User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0

--- response ---
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: private, max-age=30
Content-Length: 48

{ "bookings": [ { "id": 1, "time": "18:00" } ] }

blocks.label: Why the Host header exists
blocks.html: One IP address often serves hundreds of sites. The Host header tells the server which one you want, which is why it is the single mandatory header in HTTP/1.1. This is name-based virtual hosting.

Think of HTTP like ordering by mail. The method is what you want done (send me, create this), the path is the address on the order form, headers are the notes in the margin (how to reply, who you are), and the body is the parcel. The server mails back a numbered receipt (the status code) and its own parcel.

blocks.q: Roughly how many network round trips occur before the first HTTP request is even sent, on a fresh HTTPS connection using TLS 1.3 with DNS already cached?
options: It depends on the body size
blocks.explain: With DNS cached, you still pay one round trip for the TCP handshake and one for the TLS 1.3 handshake before any HTTP data flows — which is why connection reuse and HTTP/2 multiplexing matter so much for performance.

lessons.title: HTTP methods, status codes & semantics
glossary: The intent of a request: GET (read), POST (create/process), PUT (replace), PATCH (partial update), DELETE (remove).
A method that does not change server state; GET and HEAD are safe and may be prefetched freely.
A method where sending the same request N times has the same effect as sending it once; GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent, POST is not.
A three-digit response code: 1xx info, 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
On a 201 or 3xx response, tells the client the URL of the new or moved resource.

blocks.html: Methods and status codes are a shared vocabulary. When you honor their meaning, any client — a browser, a mobile app, a CDN, a monitoring tool — can reason about your API without reading your code. When you abuse them, everything downstream breaks in subtle ways.

blocks.label: Idempotency is not academic
blocks.html: A network can drop the response, not the request. If a client retries a non-idempotent POST /charge, it may charge twice. That is why payment APIs demand an idempotency key, and why using PUT/DELETE (idempotent) where you can makes retries safe by default.

items.label: 2xx Success
items.html: 200 OK (read/update worked, body included), 201 Created (a POST made a resource; include a Location header), 204 No Content (success, deliberately empty — common for DELETE).

items.label: 3xx Redirect
items.html: 301 Moved Permanently (update your links; cacheable), 302/307 Found/Temporary (go here for now), 304 Not Modified (your cached copy is still fresh — no body sent).

items.label: 4xx Client error
items.html: 400 Bad Request (malformed/invalid), 401 Unauthorized (you are not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (authenticated but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable, 429 Too Many Requests.

items.label: 5xx Server error
items.html: 500 Internal Server Error (your code threw), 502 Bad Gateway / 503 Service Unavailable (upstream down or overloaded), 504 Gateway Timeout.

blocks.label: 401 vs 403 — the classic mix-up
blocks.html: 401 means "I don't know who you are" — send credentials. 403 means "I know exactly who you are, and you still can't do this." Returning 403 when you mean 401 makes clients retry login pointlessly; the reverse leaks that a resource exists.

blocks.q: A user retries a request after a timeout. Which endpoint is safe to retry automatically without special handling?
blocks.explain: PUT is idempotent: replacing user 42 with the same data twice leaves the same state as doing it once. The POST endpoints are not idempotent, so blind retries risk duplicate orders, emails, or charges.

blocks.q: A logged-in user requests another user's private document and should be refused. The most correct status is…
blocks.explain: The user is authenticated (so not 401) but lacks permission — that is 403 Forbidden. Some apps deliberately return 404 to avoid confirming the document exists, a valid security trade-off, but 403 is the semantically correct default.

lessons.title: Statelessness, caching & keeping connections warm
glossary: Each HTTP request is independent; the server keeps no memory of prior requests unless the client resends context (a cookie or token).
A small key/value the server sets via Set-Cookie and the browser returns on every matching request — how sessions survive statelessness.
The header that governs whether and how long a response may be reused (max-age, no-store, private, public).
A version fingerprint of a response; the client revalidates with If-None-Match and may receive a cheap 304.
Keeping a TCP/TLS connection open (keep-alive) so subsequent requests skip the handshake cost.

blocks.html: HTTP is stateless by design: the server treats each request as if it had never seen you before. This is what lets you run twenty identical servers behind a load balancer — any of them can handle any request. State (who is logged in, what's in the cart) is reconstructed from what the client sends: a cookie or a token.

blocks.html: Because setup is expensive, the two biggest performance levers are reusing connections and caching responses. HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive; HTTP/2 goes further and multiplexes many requests over one connection, eliminating head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer.

blocks.code:
--- first response: server tags it ---
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Cache-Control: max-age=3600, public
ETag: "v3-9f2a"

--- later: client revalidates cheaply ---
GET /styles.css HTTP/1.1
If-None-Match: "v3-9f2a"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified

blocks.label: The cheapest request is the one you don't make
blocks.html: A correct Cache-Control can turn a 200-with-body into a 304-no-body — or skip the network entirely. Immutable, fingerprinted assets (app.9f2a.js) can be cached for a year with max-age=31536000, immutable, because a change ships under a new filename.

blocks.q: Why does statelessness make horizontal scaling (adding more servers) easy?
options: Because each server stores every user's session in RAM
Because any server can handle any request, since state travels with the request
blocks.explain: If the server holds no per-user memory, a load balancer can send a user's requests to any instance. The session context arrives with each request (cookie/token), so servers are interchangeable and you can add or remove them freely.

questions.q: Which HTTP method is both safe and idempotent?
questions.explain: GET neither changes state (safe) nor differs when repeated (idempotent). POST is neither; PATCH is generally neither.

questions.q: A POST that creates a resource should ideally return…
options: 200 with the list of all resources
201 with a Location header pointing to the new resource
questions.explain: 201 Created is the precise success code for creation, and the Location header tells the client where the new resource lives.

questions.q: DNS is responsible for…
options: Resolving a hostname to an IP address
questions.explain: DNS maps human-readable hostnames to IP addresses. Encryption is TLS; sessions are cookies/tokens.

questions.q: The TLS handshake exists primarily to…
options: Encrypt the channel and authenticate the server's identity
Parse the HTML into the DOM
questions.explain: TLS negotiates encryption keys and verifies the server's certificate so you know you're talking to the real server and no one can read the traffic.

questions.q: A 304 Not Modified response means…
options: The client's cached copy is still valid, so no body is sent
questions.explain: After revalidating with If-None-Match/If-Modified-Since, a 304 tells the client to reuse its cached copy — saving bandwidth by sending no body.

questions.q: Why is HTTP described as stateless?
options: Each request is independent; the server keeps no memory of prior requests by default
questions.explain: The protocol itself carries no session memory between requests. Applications rebuild state from cookies or tokens the client resends.

questions.q: Which status codes indicate the client did something wrong (as opposed to the server)? Select all that apply.
questions.explain: 4xx codes blame the request (bad data, missing auth, wrong URL). 5xx codes (500, 503) indicate the server or an upstream failed.

questions.q: What three-digit status code means the server understood the request but the user lacks permission (authenticated but not allowed)?
questions.explain: 403 Forbidden = known identity, insufficient permission. Contrast with 401, which means unauthenticated.

blocks.label: The div-soup trap
blocks.html: You can build everything from <div>, and beginners do. But a page that is all divs has no landmarks, no heading outline, and no built-in behavior — it is invisible to assistive tech and harder to style and maintain. Reach for the semantic element first; fall back to <div> only when nothing fits.

items: Exactly one <h1> per page (the page's title); never skip heading levels to get a smaller font — that's CSS's job.
Exactly one <main>; wrap independent, self-contained content in <article> and thematic groupings in <section> (which should have a heading).
Use <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation — never a clickable <div>, which loses keyboard focus and Enter/Space activation for free.

blocks.q: Why prefer <button> over a <div> with a click handler for an action?
options: A <button> is focusable, activates on Enter/Space, and is announced as a button — all for free
blocks.explain: Native <button> gives you keyboard focus, Enter/Space activation, and correct screen-reader role automatically. A clickable div requires you to re-implement all of that with tabindex, key handlers, and ARIA — and people usually forget.

lessons.title: Forms, validation & the platform
glossary: An element tying descriptive text to a control, via wrapping or for="id"; makes the text clickable and announced.
The type attribute (email, number, date, checkbox) that selects the right keyboard, UI, and built-in validation.
The browser's built-in validation from attributes like required, min, max, pattern.
The key under which a control's value is submitted; without it, a control is not submitted.
Associates a control with helper or error text so screen readers announce it.

blocks.html: Forms are where users hand you data — and where accessibility and validation matter most. The platform gives you a great deal for free if you use the right elements and attributes instead of rebuilding them in JavaScript.

blocks.code: We'll send your confirmation here.

blocks.label: type= is a feature, not decoration
blocks.html: type="email" shows an @-optimized keyboard on phones and validates the format; type="number" with min/max constrains input; autocomplete lets browsers and password managers fill fields correctly. Reaching for a plain type="text" throws all of that away.

blocks.title: Two things beginners get wrong on forms

cards.label: Missing labels
cards.html: A placeholder is not a label — it vanishes on focus and often fails contrast. Every control needs a real <label for> so it's announced and the tap target includes the text.

cards.label: Missing name
cards.html: A control without a name attribute is silently omitted from the submitted data and FormData. If "the field isn't sending," check for a missing name first.

blocks.html: Validate on the client for fast feedback, but never trust it — a malicious client can skip it entirely. The server must re-validate every field. Client validation is a courtesy; server validation is the security boundary.

blocks.q: A form field's value isn't showing up in the submitted data or FormData. The most likely cause is…
blocks.explain: Only controls with a name attribute are serialized and submitted. An id is for labels and scripting; the name is the submission key. This is one of the most common form bugs.

lessons.title: Accessibility: keyboard, screen readers & ARIA
glossary: Shorthand for accessibility (a, 11 letters, y) — building so people with disabilities can use your app.
What an element is (button, dialog, navigation); native elements have implicit roles, ARIA can set them explicitly.
The text a screen reader announces for a control, computed from labels, aria-label, or content.
The sequence in which Tab moves through interactive elements; it should follow the visual/reading order.
The luminance ratio between text and background; WCAG AA requires at least 4.5:1 for normal text.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines — the international standard, with levels A, AA (the common target), and AAA.

blocks.html: Roughly one in six people has a disability, and accessibility overlaps heavily with plain good engineering: keyboard support, clear focus, sufficient contrast, and meaningful structure help everyone. In many jurisdictions it is also a legal requirement. Treat it as a baseline, not a bonus.

items: Operable by keyboard. Every action reachable by mouse must work with Tab, Enter/Space, and arrow keys. Unplug your mouse and try your app.
Visible focus. Never do outline: none without a replacement; keyboard users must see where they are.
Sufficient contrast. Body text needs a 4.5:1 ratio (WCAG AA). Light-gray-on-white looks elegant and is unreadable to many.
Text alternatives. Meaningful images need alt; decorative images take empty alt="" so they're skipped.
Meaningful structure. Real headings, landmarks, and labels — the semantics from the last two lessons — are the backbone of screen-reader navigation.

blocks.label: The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA
blocks.html: ARIA adds semantics to elements that lack them, but native HTML already carries them. A <button> beats <div role="button" tabindex="0"> every time. Incorrect ARIA is worse than none — it actively lies to assistive tech. Use it only when no native element fits (e.g. a custom tab panel), and follow the WAI-ARIA patterns exactly.

blocks.q: You've built a custom clickable component as <div class="btn" onclick=…>. What is the correct fix for accessibility?
options: Add aria-label and call it done
Replace it with a native <button>, which is focusable, keyboard-operable, and correctly announced by default
blocks.explain: Native <button> gives keyboard focus, Enter/Space activation, and the button role for free. Reaching for a div forces you to add tabindex, key handlers, and ARIA — reinventing what the platform already does correctly.

blocks.q: A designer hands you light-gray body text at a 3:1 contrast ratio. Under WCAG AA, this…
options: Fails for normal-size text, which needs at least 4.5:1
Is fine if the font is bold
blocks.explain: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text (3:1 is only allowed for large text, roughly 18px bold or 24px regular). Low contrast is one of the most common and most impactful accessibility failures.

questions.q: Which element correctly identifies the primary content region of a page?
questions.explain: <main> is the landmark for the page's unique primary content; there should be exactly one, and screen-reader users can jump straight to it.

questions.q: The best reason to wrap an <input> in a <label> (or use for=) is…
options: It ties clickable, screen-reader-announced text to the field
It is required for the page to load
questions.explain: A properly associated label is announced by assistive tech and makes the label text part of the tap/click target — core usability and accessibility.

questions.q: A control is missing from the submitted form data. The most likely cause is…
questions.explain: Only named controls are serialized on submit. The id is for labels/scripting; the name is the submission key.

questions.q: Under WCAG AA, normal-size body text must have a contrast ratio of at least…
questions.explain: AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text; 3:1 is only permitted for large text. Low contrast excludes users with low vision.

questions.q: The 'first rule of ARIA' is…
options: Don't use ARIA if a native HTML element already has the semantics
questions.explain: Native elements carry correct semantics and behavior; incorrect ARIA misinforms assistive tech. Prefer real HTML and use ARIA only when nothing native fits.

questions.q: Client-side form validation should be treated as…
options: A UX convenience that the server must still re-check
A replacement for the name attribute
questions.explain: Clients can be bypassed, so client validation only improves UX. The server must re-validate everything — that's the real trust boundary.

questions.q: Which practices improve keyboard accessibility? Select all that apply.
options: Using outline: none with no replacement
Ensuring Tab order follows reading order
Making custom widgets operable with Enter/Space/arrows
questions.explain: Visible focus, logical Tab order, and key-operable widgets all help keyboard users. Removing focus outlines with no replacement strands them.

lessons.title: The cascade, specificity & inheritance
glossary: A pattern that targets elements: type (button), class (.btn), id (#save), attribute ([type=email]), pseudo-class (:hover).
The algorithm that resolves conflicting declarations using origin/importance, then specificity, then source order.
A three-number score (id, class, type) computed per selector to break conflicts before source order is consulted.
Some properties (color, font) pass from parent to child; others (margin, border) do not.
A flag that lifts a declaration into a higher-priority origin layer, bypassing normal specificity — a last resort.

blocks.html: When two rules set the same property on the same element, the browser resolves the conflict with a precise, learnable algorithm — not with "whatever came last" folklore. Master it and "my CSS won't apply" stops being mysterious.

blocks.title: The cascade, in resolution order
steps: 1. Origin & importance
Author styles beat browser defaults; an !important author rule beats a normal author rule. This layer is checked first.
2. Specificity
Among rules in the same layer, the higher specificity score wins. Computed as (ids, classes, types).
3. Source order
Only if specificity ties does the last declaration in the source win.

blocks.html: Specificity is counted as three columns — (id, class, type) — where class also covers attribute selectors and pseudo-classes, and type covers pseudo-elements. Inline style= ranks above all selectors; the universal selector * counts as zero.

blocks.label: Specificity is columnar, not a sum
blocks.html: Compare left to right: a single id (1,0,0) beats any number of classes (0,255,0). So #save defeats .toolbar .primary .btn.big. This is why deep id-based selectors are so hard to override — and why component systems keep specificity low and flat.

blocks.q: Rule A is #save { color: red } (1,0,0). Rule B is .toolbar .btn.primary { color: blue } (0,3,0). Which wins?
options: blue — three classes outweigh one id
red — a single id column beats any number of classes
blocks.explain: Specificity is compared column by column, most significant first. The id column (1 vs 0) is decided before classes are even considered, so red wins regardless of source order or class count.

blocks.label: Why !important is a trap
blocks.html: !important wins by jumping origin layers, so people fight it with more !important, and specificity stops meaning anything. The professional fix for "it won't override" is a flat, consistent class system — not escalation. Reserve !important for genuinely un-overridable utilities or third-party overrides.

content-box (default) sizes only the content; border-box includes padding and border in the declared width.
The default block-and-inline layout before you change display.
A one-dimensional layout system distributing items along a single axis (row or column).

blocks.html: The box model is the mental model for all spacing: content is wrapped by padding, then border, then margin. By default width measures only the content, so adding padding makes boxes wider than you declared — which surprises everyone.

blocks.explain: A wrapping grid of rows and columns is inherently two-dimensional, which is Grid's job. auto-fill + minmax creates responsive columns with no media queries. Flexbox can wrap but doesn't align items into a clean two-dimensional grid as naturally.

blocks.q: In a flex row (default flex-direction), align-items: center centers items…
options: Only if there is one item
blocks.explain: In a row the main axis is horizontal (controlled by justify-content) and the cross axis is vertical (controlled by align-items). So align-items: center centers vertically.

lessons.title: Responsive design & design systems with custom properties
glossary: A conditional block of CSS that applies only when a condition (e.g. min-width) is met.
Writing base styles for small screens, then layering enhancements with min-width queries.
A unit relative to the root font-size; scales with the user's browser text-size preference (respect accessibility).
A CSS variable declared as --name and read with var(--name); cascades and can be themed at runtime.
A named design value (color, spacing, radius) reused everywhere so the system stays consistent.
A media feature exposing the user's OS light/dark preference.

blocks.html: Responsive design means one codebase that adapts to any viewport. The professional default is mobile-first: write the simplest, single-column layout as the base, then use min-width media queries to progressively enhance for larger screens. This keeps the base lean and the overrides additive.

blocks.label: Use rem, not px, for type
blocks.html: Sizing text in rem respects a user who bumped their browser's default font size for readability; hard-coded px ignores them. Accessibility and responsiveness overlap here — relative units are the accessible default.
Hard-coding #4f7cff in forty places is how stylesheets rot. Custom properties let you name values once — as design tokens — and theme the entire app, including dark mode, from a single place.

blocks.label: Why this is a professional move
blocks.html: A client says "make the blue a touch greener." With tokens you edit one line and the whole app updates consistently; without them you hunt through forty files and miss three. Tokens are the difference between a hobby stylesheet and a maintainable design system — and unlike Sass variables, custom properties are live at runtime, so JavaScript can flip a theme instantly.

blocks.q: The main advantage of CSS custom properties over hard-coded values is…
options: They make CSS run as JavaScript
You name a value once and can theme/override it everywhere, at runtime
They eliminate the need for classes
blocks.explain: Custom properties centralize design tokens for consistency and enable runtime theming (like dark mode or a live accent change) from one place — something static values and even preprocessor variables can't do at runtime.

blocks.q: Mobile-first responsive CSS writes base styles for … and adds min-width media queries for larger screens.
blocks.explain: Mobile-first starts with the small-screen layout as the base and enhances upward with min-width queries, keeping the base simple and overrides additive.

questions.q: The specificity of #save .btn is…
questions.explain: One id (#save) and one class (.btn) gives (1,1,0). The id column dominates any class-only selector.

questions.q: box-sizing: border-box makes the declared width…
questions.explain: border-box folds padding and border into the width, so a 300px box stays 300px wide regardless of padding — predictable sizing.

questions.q: You need rows AND columns that align in two dimensions (a dashboard). The right tool is…
questions.explain: Grid is the two-dimensional layout system; Flexbox handles a single axis at a time.

questions.q: A single id selector, in the cascade, beats…
questions.explain: Specificity compares columns left to right, so one id (1,0,0) outranks even (0,50,0). It does not, however, beat an inline style.

questions.q: Mobile-first means your base styles target…
options: Small screens, enhanced upward with min-width queries
questions.explain: Base = mobile; min-width media queries add complexity for larger viewports, keeping overrides additive.

questions.q: Custom properties (CSS variables) are declared and read as…
questions.explain: Declared as --name (typically on :root) and read with var(--name), with an optional fallback: var(--name, default).

questions.q: Reaching for !important to make a style apply usually signals…
options: A specificity conflict better solved with a flatter class system
questions.explain: !important escalates origin layers and starts arms races. The real fix is consistent, low-specificity selectors so nothing needs to override anything by force.

modules.title: JavaScript: The Language & the Event Loop
modules.tagline: Types and coercion, functions and closures, and the single-threaded runtime that ties it together.
objectives: Use JavaScript's types, strict equality, and control flow without falling into coercion traps.
Explain scope, closures, and this, and use them deliberately.
Transform data with map/filter/reduce and reason about their time complexity.
Describe the event loop, call stack, and the microtask vs macrotask queues, and predict execution order.

lessons.title: Types, coercion & equality
glossary: An immutable basic value: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol, bigint.
Objects and arrays, held by reference; two variables can point at the same object.
Automatic type conversion, e.g. when == compares a number to a string.
=== compares value and type with no coercion; always prefer it over ==.
How a value behaves in a boolean context; falsy = false, 0, -0, "", null, undefined, NaN.
Not-a-Number, the only value not equal to itself; test with Number.isNaN().

blocks.html: JavaScript has just a handful of types, but its implicit coercion rules are where hours are lost. The cure is small and absolute: use ===, know your falsy values, and never compare types you didn't convert on purpose.

blocks.code:
typeof "hi"      // "string"
typeof 42        // "number"
typeof true      // "boolean"
typeof undefined // "undefined"
typeof null      // "object"  <-- a famous historical bug
typeof {}        // "object"
typeof []        // "object"  (use Array.isArray to be sure)
typeof function(){} // "function"

blocks.label: === always, == never
blocks.html: Loose == coerces before comparing, producing gems like 0 == "" (true), 0 == "0" (true), but "" == "0" (false) — intransitive nonsense. Strict === compares value and type with no surprises. The single exception some teams allow is x == null to catch both null and undefined; otherwise, always strict.

head: Expression
== result
=== result
Why
rows: NaN is never equal to anything

blocks.label: The falsy list is finite — memorize it
blocks.html: Exactly these are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else — including "0", "false", [], and {} — is truthy. This is why if (items.length) works but if ([]) is always true.

blocks.q: Why does the code if (user.age) skip a legitimately zero-age user?
options: Because 0 is falsy, so the block is skipped
blocks.explain: 0 is one of the falsy values, so if (user.age) treats a real age of 0 as 'missing'. When 0 (or empty string) is a valid value, test explicitly: if (user.age != null) or if (Number.isFinite(user.age)).

lessons.title: Functions, scope, closures & this
glossary: The region where a binding is visible; JavaScript has function scope and block scope ({ } with let/const).
A function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was defined, even after that scope returns.
Declarations are processed before execution; function declarations and var are hoisted, let/const are in a temporal dead zone.
The call-time receiver of a function; depends on how the function is called, not where it's defined — except in arrow functions.
A concise function that has no own this; it captures this from the surrounding scope.
A function that takes or returns another function (map, filter, addEventListener).

blocks.html: Functions are JavaScript's core abstraction, and two features trip up everyone who skips them: closures (why a returned function still 'remembers' data) and this (why a method loses its receiver when detached). Learn them deliberately and whole categories of bugs disappear.

A closure is a backpack. When a function is created, it zips up the variables it can see and carries that backpack wherever it goes. Even after the outer function has returned and its stack frame is gone, the inner function still reaches into the backpack. That's how event handlers and callbacks 'remember' the data they were set up with.

blocks.label: this is about the call site
blocks.html: In a regular function, this is whatever is left of the dot at call time. So const f = obj.method; f() loses obj and this becomes undefined (strict mode). Fixes: call it as obj.method(), bind it (obj.method.bind(obj)), or use an arrow function, which has no own this and captures the surrounding one — which is exactly why arrows are ideal for callbacks inside a class method.

blocks.q: You pass this.handleClick (a regular method) as a callback and inside it this is undefined. The idiomatic fix is…
options: Define it as an arrow function (or bind it) so it captures the instance's this
blocks.explain: A detached regular method loses its receiver. An arrow function has no own this and captures the enclosing this (the instance); binding achieves the same. This is the canonical callback-loses-this bug.

blocks.q: What makes a closure useful for data privacy?
options: The inner function can access outer variables that nothing else can reach
blocks.explain: Variables in the enclosing scope are reachable only by the inner function(s) that closed over them — no outside code can touch them. That's genuine private state, the basis of the module pattern.

lessons.title: Arrays, higher-order functions & complexity
glossary: Returns a new array applying a function to each element; O(n).
Returns a new array of elements passing a predicate; O(n).
Collapses an array to a single accumulated value; O(n).
Producing new values instead of mutating existing ones — safer for shared state.
How an operation's cost grows with input size: O(1) constant, O(n) linear, O(n²) quadratic.
Built-in collections with O(1) average lookup, unlike scanning an array (O(n)).

blocks.html: Real apps mostly shuttle lists of objects around. The higher-order array methods replace error-prone loops with declarative transformations — and knowing their Big-O tells you when a convenient one-liner quietly becomes a performance problem.

blocks.code:
const bookings = [
  { id: 1, name: "Ada", time: 18, paid: true },
  { id: 2, name: "Ben", time: 19, paid: false },
  { id: 3, name: "Cy",  time: 18, paid: true },
];

const names = bookings.map(b => b.name);            // ["Ada","Ben","Cy"]
const at18  = bookings.filter(b => b.time === 18);  // 2 items
const paid  = bookings.reduce((n, b) => n + (b.paid ? 1 : 0), 0); // 2

blocks.label: The accidental O(n²)
blocks.html: It's tempting to write a.filter(x => b.includes(x.id)). But includes scans b every time, so filtering an n-item list against an n-item list is O(n²) — fine for 100 items, catastrophic for 100,000. Build a Set of ids first (const s = new Set(b); a.filter(x => s.has(x.id))) to get O(n) with O(1) lookups.

blocks.label: Prefer immutable transforms for shared state
blocks.html: map/filter/reduce return new arrays and never mutate the source, which keeps state predictable — the same property React and Redux rely on to detect changes cheaply. Reserve mutating methods (sort, splice, reverse) for local, throwaway data, or copy first: [...arr].sort().

blocks.q: You need to keep only items whose id appears in a 50,000-element list of allowed ids, called many times. The efficient approach is…
options: Build new Set(allowed) once, then filter with set.has(x.id) — O(n)
Use a for-loop, which is always faster
blocks.explain: includes is an O(n) scan, so filtering with it is O(n²). Converting allowed to a Set gives O(1) membership tests, making the whole filter O(n). Choosing the right data structure, not the loop syntax, is what changes the complexity class.

blocks.q: Which array method mutates the original array in place?
blocks.explain: sort (like splice and reverse) mutates the array it's called on. map, filter, and reduce all return new values and leave the source untouched — copy first with [...arr].sort() if you need to preserve the original.

lessons.title: The event loop: stack, tasks & microtasks
glossary: The stack of function calls currently executing; JavaScript runs on a single thread with one stack.
Occupying the single thread so nothing else — rendering, clicks — can run until it finishes.
A unit of work queued by timers, I/O, or events; one runs per loop iteration.
A higher-priority job (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask); the whole microtask queue drains after each task, before rendering.
The coordinator that runs a task, drains microtasks, optionally renders, then repeats.

blocks.html: JavaScript is single-threaded: one call stack, one thing at a time. Yet it handles clicks, timers, and network responses without freezing. The trick is the event loop, which schedules asynchronous callbacks to run when the stack is empty — and the order it uses is a common interview question and a real source of bugs.

blocks.caption: The runtime: async work goes to Web APIs; the loop empties the stack, drains ALL microtas

blocks.label: Don't block the loop
blocks.html: Because there's one thread, a long synchronous loop (say, sorting a million items or a busy-wait) freezes clicks, scrolling, and rendering until it finishes. For heavy work, break it into chunks, defer with setTimeout, or offload to a Web Worker (a real second thread). "Async" doesn't mean parallel — it means non-blocking scheduling on the same thread.

cards.label: Single-threaded
cards.html: Your JS never runs two lines at once. Concurrency comes from the platform (network, timers) doing work off-thread and queuing callbacks.

cards.label: Microtasks jump the line
cards.html: A resolved promise's .then runs before the next setTimeout, even a 0ms one. Awaiting in a loop can starve rendering if you're not careful.

blocks.q: What does this log, in order? console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4);
blocks.explain: Synchronous lines run first: 1 then 4. Then the event loop drains the microtask queue (the promise: 3) before taking the next macrotask (the timer: 2). So the order is 1, 4, 3, 2 — microtasks always beat a 0ms timeout.

blocks.q: Why does a heavy synchronous for-loop make the whole page unresponsive?
options: It occupies the single thread, so rendering and event handlers can't run until it finishes
blocks.explain: JavaScript shares one thread with the rendering and event-handling work of the page. A long synchronous computation keeps the call stack busy, so nothing else — paint, clicks, scroll — can happen until it returns. Chunk the work or use a Web Worker.

questions.q: Which operator compares value and type without coercion?
questions.explain: === is strict equality; == coerces types and yields intransitive surprises like 0 == "".

questions.q: Which of these is truthy?
questions.explain: The string "0" is a non-empty string and therefore truthy. 0, "", and NaN are all falsy.

questions.q: A closure lets an inner function…
options: Remember variables from the scope where it was defined
questions.explain: A closure retains access to its defining scope's variables even after that scope has returned — the basis of private state and stateful callbacks.

questions.q: In a regular (non-arrow) function, this is determined by…
options: How the function is called (the call site)
questions.explain: Regular functions bind this at call time based on the receiver; arrow functions instead capture this lexically from their surrounding scope.

questions.q: Filtering an array with .includes() against another array is what complexity?
questions.explain: includes is an O(n) scan performed for each of n items, giving O(n²). A Set reduces membership tests to O(1), making it O(n).

questions.q: After synchronous code finishes, the event loop next runs…
options: All queued microtasks (e.g. promise .then) before any macrotask
questions.explain: The microtask queue is drained completely after each task and before the next macrotask or render — so promise continuations beat a 0ms timer.

questions.q: Which array method mutates its array in place?
questions.explain: splice mutates the original array (as do sort and reverse). map/filter/reduce return new values.

questions.q: What is the one value in JavaScript that is not equal to itself (NaN === NaN is false)? Answer with the three-letter identifier.
questions.explain: NaN is never equal to anything, including itself; use Number.isNaN() to test for it.

lessons.title: From HTML to the DOM, and the DOM API
glossary: Document Object Model — the browser's live, in-memory tree of objects built by parsing HTML.
Any point in the tree: an element node, a text node, a comment, etc.
Selects the first element matching a CSS selector; querySelectorAll returns all as a static NodeList.
textContent sets plain text safely; innerHTML parses a string as HTML (and can inject scripts/markup).
A lightweight, off-screen container you can build up and insert once to avoid repeated reflows.

blocks.html: When the browser parses your HTML, it builds the DOM: a tree of objects, one per node, that JavaScript can read and mutate at runtime. The HTML file is the blueprint; the DOM is the living building. All interactivity is, ultimately, DOM manipulation.

blocks.title: The tree from a booking form — tap each node

items.label: html
items.html: The document root; contains head and body.

items.label: body
items.html: Everything visible; parent of header and main.

items.label: form#booking
items.html: An element node with id 'booking'. Grab it with document.getElementById('booking').

items.label: input / select
items.html: Leaf-ish nodes whose .value property holds what the user typed or chose.

items.label: #text
items.html: Text nodes hold the actual characters between tags — they're nodes too.

blocks.label: innerHTML is an XSS vector
blocks.html: el.innerHTML = userInput parses the string as HTML, so a value like <img src=x onerror=steal()> executes. For untrusted data use textContent (or build nodes and set .textContent). We'll return to this in the security module — for now: never put user input into innerHTML.

blocks.q: You want to display a user-provided display name in a heading, safely. You should assign it to…
blocks.explain: textContent sets the value as literal text, so any HTML in the user's name is shown, not executed. innerHTML (and the HTML-parsing insert methods) would run injected markup/scripts — a classic XSS bug.

lessons.title: Events: propagation & delegation
glossary: A signal the browser dispatches (click, input, submit, keydown) that you can listen for.
The event travels root → target first; listeners with {capture:true} fire here.
After reaching the target, the event travels target → root; most listeners fire here.
Attaching one listener to a common ancestor and using event.target to handle many children.
Cancels the browser's default action (form submit, link navigation).
Stops the event from continuing to bubble/capture to other elements.

blocks.html: An event doesn't just fire on the element you clicked — it travels. Understanding the three phases (capture → target → bubble) explains why a click on a button also triggers a listener on its container, and unlocks the most useful pattern in front-end code: delegation.

blocks.label: Why delegation is the pro default
blocks.html: Delegation means fewer listeners (memory + setup cost), and it automatically covers elements added after you wired things up — no re-binding on every render. This is exactly how frameworks attach a single root listener and route events internally. Reach for it whenever you'd otherwise loop and attach.

cards.label: preventDefault()
cards.html: Cancels the browser's default action — stops a form's full-page submit or a link's navigation. Does NOT stop the event from bubbling.

cards.label: stopPropagation()
cards.html: Stops the event from travelling to other listeners up (or down) the tree. Does NOT cancel the default action. They're independent — reach for the one you actually need.

blocks.q: You render a list that gains new items over time and want each item clickable. The most robust approach is…
options: Attach a click listener to each item after every render
Attach one click listener to the list container and use event.target.closest('li')
Poll the DOM in a setInterval
blocks.explain: Event delegation puts a single listener on the stable parent and reads which child was clicked from the bubbling event. It covers items added later automatically and uses far fewer listeners than binding each element.

blocks.q: In a form's submit handler, e.preventDefault() is used to…
options: Cancel the browser's default full-page submit so your JS can handle it
blocks.explain: preventDefault cancels the default action (here the page-reloading submit). It's independent of propagation — stopPropagation is the one that halts bubbling.

lessons.title: The rendering pipeline & performance
glossary: The DOM combined with computed styles, used to lay out and paint what's visible.
Recomputing element geometry (positions, sizes); triggered by size/position/DOM changes.
Redrawing pixels without changing layout (e.g. a color change).
Repeatedly interleaving DOM reads and writes, forcing many synchronous reflows in a row.
Combining painted layers on the GPU; transform/opacity changes can skip layout and paint.

blocks.html: Changing the DOM isn't free. The browser runs a pipeline — style → layout (reflow) → paint → composite — and certain changes force expensive stages to re-run. Knowing which is the difference between a smooth 60fps interface and a janky one.

blocks.title: The rendering pipeline
steps: Style
Match CSS rules to nodes and compute final styles for each element.
Layout (reflow)
Calculate the geometry — where every box goes and how big it is. Triggered by size, position, or DOM-structure changes.
Paint
Fill in pixels: text, colors, borders, shadows into layers.
Composite
Assemble layers on the GPU. transform and opacity can be composited without re-layout or repaint.

blocks.label: Layout thrashing
blocks.html: Reading a layout property (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect) forces the browser to flush any pending layout now. If you interleave read → write → read → write in a loop, you force a synchronous reflow each iteration — turning an O(n) loop into O(n) reflows. Batch all reads, then all writes.

blocks.html: This connects to the pattern behind every framework: keep the source of truth in state, write a render() that draws the DOM from that state, and let events update state and re-render. Frameworks like React add a virtual DOM diff so only the changed nodes touch the real DOM — an optimization of exactly this idea.

blocks.q: Why does reading el.offsetHeight inside a loop that also writes styles hurt performance?
options: Each read forces the browser to flush pending layout, causing a synchronous reflow every iteration
blocks.explain: Layout-reading properties force the browser to recompute layout immediately so the value is accurate. Interleaving reads and writes makes it reflow on every pass (layout thrashing); batching all reads then all writes collapses it to one reflow.

blocks.q: In the state → render pattern, an event handler should…
options: Directly edit many DOM nodes by hand
Update the state, then call render()
Do nothing until the next paint
blocks.explain: Handlers mutate state and re-render, keeping the DOM a pure function of state. That predictability is exactly what React, Vue, and Svelte formalize — and it makes UI bugs far easier to reason about.

questions.q: The DOM is best described as…
options: The raw HTML text file on disk
A live, in-memory tree of objects the browser builds from HTML
questions.explain: The browser parses HTML into the DOM tree; JavaScript reads and mutates it to create interactivity.

questions.q: To display untrusted user text safely, assign it to…
questions.explain: textContent inserts literal text and cannot execute injected markup; the HTML-parsing paths are XSS-prone.

questions.q: Event delegation works because events…
options: Bubble up from the target through its ancestors
questions.explain: A single listener on an ancestor catches bubbling events from many descendants and reads event.target to act — fewer listeners and automatic coverage of new elements.

questions.q: preventDefault() and stopPropagation() differ in that…
options: preventDefault cancels the default action; stopPropagation halts event travel
questions.explain: They're independent: one cancels the browser's default behavior, the other stops the event from reaching other listeners.

questions.q: Which CSS change can typically be handled by compositing alone, skipping layout and paint?
questions.explain: transform and opacity can be composited on the GPU without reflow or repaint, which is why animations should prefer them over animating top/left/width.

questions.q: Layout thrashing is caused by…
options: Interleaving DOM reads and writes so each read forces a synchronous reflow
questions.explain: Reading layout properties flushes pending layout; interleaving reads and writes forces repeated reflows. Batch reads then writes to fix it.

questions.q: In the state→render pattern, the single source of truth is…
options: A state variable that render() reads from
questions.explain: State is authoritative; render() derives the DOM from it and events mutate state then re-render — the core idea behind modern frameworks.

lessons.title: JSON, data modeling & reference semantics
glossary: JavaScript Object Notation — a text format for data: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null.
JSON.stringify turns objects into text; JSON.parse turns text back into objects.
Objects and arrays are shared by reference; primitives are copied by value.
A shallow copy ({...o}) duplicates the top level only; a deep copy (structuredClone) duplicates nested structures too.
The agreed shape of your data — its fields, types, and constraints.

blocks.html: JSON is the lingua franca of the web — how the frontend, backend, and APIs exchange data. It looks like JavaScript object literals but is pure, language-agnostic text, with a tiny grammar: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null (no functions, no dates, no comments).

blocks.label: The aliasing gotcha
blocks.html: Objects and arrays are held by reference. const b = a makes b point at the same object, so mutating b mutates a. To copy: {...a} / [...a] for a shallow copy, or structuredClone(a) for a deep one. This single misunderstanding is behind a huge share of 'my state changed by itself' bugs.

blocks.label: A quick equality caution
blocks.html: {} === {} is false — reference types compare by identity, not contents. To compare data, compare fields explicitly or compare JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b) (order-sensitive, and it silently drops functions/undefined — use knowingly).

blocks.q: const b = a where a is an array, then b.push(9). What happens to a?
options: a is unchanged; b is an independent copy
a also gains 9, because b references the same array
blocks.explain: Arrays are reference types; b = a copies the reference, not the array. Both names point to one array, so push through either is visible through both. Use [...a] or structuredClone(a) to actually copy.

lessons.title: Promises, async/await & error handling
glossary: Runs line by line, blocking the thread until each finishes.
Starts work now and continues later via a callback/promise, without blocking.
An object representing a future value: pending → fulfilled or rejected.
Syntax that lets promise-based code read top-to-bottom; await pauses only the async function, not the thread.
A promise's failure path; unhandled rejections are a common source of silent bugs.

blocks.html: Network and disk operations take time. If JavaScript waited synchronously the UI would freeze (remember: one thread). Instead, async work returns a promise — a placeholder for a value that arrives later — and async/await lets you write it as if it were linear, while the event loop keeps the page responsive.

blocks.label: fetch only rejects on network failure
blocks.html: A common trap: fetch does not throw on 404 or 500 — those are successful HTTP exchanges from the browser's view. The promise only rejects if the request can't complete at all (offline, DNS, CORS). So you must check res.ok yourself and throw, or your error handling silently misses server errors.

blocks.title: A promise's lifecycle
steps: Pending
Created; the async work is in flight.
Fulfilled
Resolved with a value; .then / the awaited expression receives it.
Rejected
Failed with a reason; .catch / a surrounding try-catch receives it.
Settled
Fulfilled or rejected — it will never change again.

blocks.label: Always handle the failure path
blocks.html: Beginners write the happy path only. Professionals wrap awaits in try/catch, check res.ok, and show the user something sensible (a retry, a message). An unhandledrejection is the async equivalent of an uncaught exception — never leave one dangling.

blocks.q: await can be used…
options: Inside an async function (or at module top level)
blocks.explain: await is valid inside an async function or at a module's top level. It pauses that function until the promise settles, without blocking the single thread.

blocks.q: Your fetch to a URL returns 500, but your catch block never runs. Why?
options: fetch resolves on any completed HTTP exchange; you must check res.ok and throw yourself
blocks.explain: fetch only rejects on network-level failure, not on HTTP error status. A 500 is a completed response, so the promise fulfills. Check res.ok and throw to route server errors into your catch.

lessons.title: Concurrency, sequencing & persistence
glossary: Runs promises concurrently and resolves to an array of results, rejecting if any one rejects.
Like all, but waits for every promise and reports each outcome, never short-circuiting.
Awaiting one call, then the next — correct for dependencies, wasteful for independent work.
Synchronous browser key/value storage that persists across reloads; strings only, ~5MB.
Loading saved state back into the app on startup.

blocks.html: await is easy to misuse. Awaiting independent calls one after another makes them run in series, so three 200ms calls take 600ms instead of 200ms. When calls don't depend on each other, launch them together with Promise.all.

blocks.label: Promise.all is all-or-nothing
blocks.html: Promise.all rejects the moment any input rejects, discarding the others' results. When you want every result regardless (e.g. a dashboard where one widget can fail), use Promise.allSettled, which returns a status for each.

For many small apps, the browser is enough storage. localStorage keeps key/value strings across reloads — exactly how a course app remembers your progress. Wrap it defensively: it can throw (private mode, quota) and it only stores strings, so serialize with JSON.

blocks.label: When to graduate to a server
blocks.html: localStorage is per-device, per-browser, synchronous, and untrusted (users can edit it). It's perfect for preferences and single-user data. The moment data must be shared across devices/users, or must be trusted or secured, you need a backend and a database — the next modules.

blocks.q: You need a user, their posts, and their stats — none depends on the others. The fastest correct approach is…
options: Launch all three with Promise.all and await the array
blocks.explain: Independent calls should run concurrently. Promise.all fires them together so the total time is the slowest single call, not the sum. Sequential await only makes sense when a later call needs an earlier call's result.

blocks.q: localStorage can store…
options: Only strings, so you JSON.stringify objects first
blocks.explain: localStorage holds strings; serialize objects with JSON.stringify to store and JSON.parse to read. It also persists across reloads and is synchronous, so avoid huge writes on the main thread.

questions.q: JSON.parse is the inverse of…
questions.explain: stringify serializes objects to text; parse deserializes text back into objects.

questions.q: const b = a (a is an object), then b.x = 9. What is a.x?
options: 9, because b references the same object
questions.explain: Objects are shared by reference; b and a name the same object, so writing through b is visible through a. Copy with {...a} or structuredClone(a).

questions.q: A shallow copy {...obj} fails to isolate…
options: Nested objects/arrays, which remain shared by reference
questions.explain: Spread copies only the top level; nested references are still shared. Use structuredClone for a deep copy.

questions.q: fetch() rejects its promise when…
options: The request can't complete at all (offline, DNS, CORS)
questions.explain: fetch resolves for any completed HTTP exchange, including 4xx/5xx. Only a network-level failure rejects — so check res.ok yourself.

questions.q: To run three independent async calls concurrently and get all results, use…
questions.explain: Promise.all launches them together and resolves to an array; total time is the slowest call rather than the sum.

questions.q: The difference between Promise.all and Promise.allSettled is…
options: all rejects on the first failure; allSettled waits for every promise and reports each outcome
questions.explain: all short-circuits on the first rejection; allSettled never short-circuits and returns a status object per promise — use it when one failure shouldn't sink the rest.

questions.q: Wrapping localStorage access in try/catch matters because…
options: Storage can be blocked or full and shouldn't crash the app
questions.explain: setItem can throw in private mode or when over quota; catching keeps the app running gracefully. Also remember it only stores strings.

lessons.title: Servers & REST API design
glossary: A long-running program that listens for requests and returns responses.
A specific method + path the server handles (GET /bookings).
A convention mapping resources to URLs and HTTP verbs to CRUD operations.
Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four persistent-data operations.
A function that runs on every (or many) requests: logging, body parsing, auth.
One that can be safely retried; align verbs (PUT/DELETE) with this property.

blocks.html: A server is just a program that waits for requests and answers them. REST is a widely used convention: model your domain as resources (nouns), give each a URL, and map HTTP verbs to CRUD. Follow it and your API becomes predictable to anyone who knows HTTP.

blocks.label: URLs are nouns, verbs are HTTP methods
blocks.html: Design smell: POST /createBooking or GET /deleteBooking?id=42. The verb belongs in the method, not the path, and a GET must never change state (a crawler could delete your data). Keep paths as resource nouns: /bookings/42.

blocks.q: Which is the RESTful way to create a booking?
options: POST /bookings with a JSON body, returning 201
blocks.explain: Create maps to POST on the collection resource (/bookings), with the data in the body, returning 201 Created (ideally with a Location header). GET must never create/modify, and the verb lives in the method, not the path.

glossary: The browser API for making HTTP requests, returning a promise.
The tuple scheme + host + port; two URLs share an origin only if all three match.
The browser rule that scripts may freely read responses only from their own origin.
Cross-Origin Resource Sharing — response headers by which a server opts specific other origins in.
An automatic OPTIONS request the browser sends before certain cross-origin requests to check permission.

blocks.html: The frontend talks to your API with fetch. Reading is a GET; creating is a POST with a JSON body and the right Content-Type. Surface failures to the user rather than swallowing them.

The browser enforces the same-origin policy: JavaScript on myapp.com may send a request to api.other.com, but the browser hides the response unless that server explicitly allows your origin via CORS headers. For some requests the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS to ask permission.

blocks.label: CORS is not a bug in your fetch
blocks.html: A CORS error means the server didn't send Access-Control-Allow-Origin for your origin. You cannot fix it in the frontend — you fix it on the server you control (add the header) or route through your own backend as a proxy. And note: CORS protects users, it is not server-side authentication — a non-browser client (curl, your server) ignores it entirely.

blocks.q: Your frontend on app.com gets a CORS error calling api.other.com. Where is the fix?
options: On the server, by sending Access-Control-Allow-Origin for your origin (or proxy through your own backend)
blocks.explain: The same-origin policy is enforced by the browser but the permission is granted by the server via CORS headers. You add the allow-origin header on the API you control, or call it from your own backend, which isn't subject to browser CORS.

lessons.title: Auth & the security non-negotiables
glossary: Determining what you're allowed to do (permissions).
A one-way transform (bcrypt, argon2) applied to passwords with a per-user salt; never reversible.
A signed credential the client presents to prove an authenticated session.
Cross-Site Scripting — injecting attacker script into a page, usually via unescaped user input.
Cross-Site Request Forgery — tricking a logged-in user's browser into making an unwanted state-changing request.
A secret (API key, DB URL) kept out of code, read from process.env at runtime.

blocks.html: Security is where sloppy code gets real people hurt. You don't need to be a specialist, but a professional never ships without the non-negotiables below. Start with the distinction that trips up beginners: authentication is who you are; authorization is what you may do. A logged-in user (authenticated) still must be checked for permission (authorized) on every sensitive action.

blocks.label: The frontend is public
blocks.html: Anything in your frontend JavaScript can be read by anyone (View Source, DevTools). API keys, DB URLs, and signing secrets must live on the server in environment variables. Committing a paid API key to a repo or bundling it into client code is a classic, expensive mistake — bots scan public repos and drain keys within hours.

blocks.title: The three vulnerabilities every web dev must know

items.label: XSS
items.html: Cross-Site Scripting. User input rendered as HTML runs as script (innerHTML = comment). Defense: escape/encode on output, use textContent, and set a Content-Security-Policy. This is why we never put untrusted data in innerHTML.

items.label: CSRF
items.html: Cross-Site Request Forgery. A malicious page makes the victim's browser POST to your app using their existing cookie. Defense: anti-CSRF tokens and SameSite=Lax/Strict cookies so the cookie isn't sent on cross-site requests.

items.label: Injection
items.html: SQL/command injection. User input concatenated into a query or shell command executes as code. Defense: parameterized queries (placeholders), never string concatenation. (Full treatment in the database module.)

blocks.label: Store tokens carefully
blocks.html: A session token in localStorage is readable by any XSS payload. Storing it in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie keeps JavaScript from reading it (mitigating token theft via XSS) at the cost of needing CSRF defenses. There's no free lunch — know the trade-off you're choosing.

blocks.q: How should user passwords be stored?
options: As plain text for easy password reset
blocks.explain: Store only a per-user salted one-way hash; verify by hashing the attempt and comparing. You can never (and should never be able to) recover the original — password reset works by issuing a new one, not retrieving the old.

blocks.q: Rendering a user's comment with element.innerHTML = comment risks which attack?
blocks.explain: Assigning untrusted input to innerHTML parses it as HTML, so an injected <script> or onerror handler runs — cross-site scripting. Use textContent, escape on output, and add a Content-Security-Policy.

blocks.q: A SameSite=Strict cookie primarily defends against…
options: CSRF, by not sending the cookie on cross-site requests
blocks.explain: SameSite restricts when the browser attaches the cookie to cross-site requests, so a forged request from another site won't carry the victim's session cookie — a core CSRF defense.

blocks.title: Go deeper
items: OWASP Top Ten
The industry's canonical list of the most common web risks; read the entries for injection, XSS, and access control.

Concise, authoritative defenses for each vulnerability.
MDN — Content Security Policy (CSP)
A defense-in-depth header that blocks injected scripts even if escaping is missed.

questions.q: In REST, GET /bookings/42 should…
questions.explain: GET reads and must be side-effect-free; the path identifies the specific resource. A GET that mutates state is a serious design (and security) error.

questions.q: A CORS error is resolved…
options: On the server, by allowing the calling origin (or via your own proxy)
questions.explain: The browser enforces same-origin; the server grants exceptions with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. You fix it server-side or proxy through a backend, which isn't subject to browser CORS.

questions.q: Passwords must be stored as…
questions.explain: Hash with a per-user salt and a modern algorithm; never store or log the plaintext, and never rely on reversible encoding like Base64.

questions.q: Authentication vs authorization: authentication is…
questions.explain: Authentication establishes identity (login); authorization decides permissions. Both must be checked — a valid login doesn't imply access to a given resource.

questions.q: Putting untrusted user input into element.innerHTML risks…
questions.explain: innerHTML parses the string as HTML, executing injected markup/scripts — cross-site scripting. Use textContent and escape on output.

questions.q: A SameSite cookie attribute helps defend against…
questions.explain: SameSite limits sending the cookie on cross-site requests, blunting forged requests from other origins — a CSRF defense.

questions.q: API secrets in a deployed app belong…
options: In environment variables on the server
questions.explain: Frontend code is public. Secrets live in server-side environment variables, never committed or shipped to the browser.

questions.q: Which are effective defenses against the named attacks? Select all that apply.
options: SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens against CSRF
questions.explain: Parameterized queries, output escaping/CSP, and SameSite+tokens each defend against their respective attacks. Base64 is encoding, not security, and offers no protection.

lessons.title: Relational vs document, schema & normalization
glossary: Data in tables of typed columns, related by keys, queried with SQL (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite).
Flexible JSON-like documents grouped in collections (MongoDB, Firestore).
The defined shape: tables, columns, types, and constraints.
A column uniquely identifying each row (usually id).
A column referencing another table's primary key, enforcing a relationship.
Structuring tables so each fact lives in exactly one place, avoiding duplication and update anomalies.

blocks.html: A database is durable, queryable, multi-user, trustworthy storage — everything localStorage is not. The central choice: relational (typed tables related by keys, queried with SQL) versus document (flexible JSON documents). For most business apps, relational is the safe default.

tabs.label: Relational
tabs.html: Structured, related data — users, orders, bookings, payments. Strong consistency, typed columns, powerful JOINs, transactions. The default for anything with relationships. Postgres is the modern favorite.

tabs.label: Document
tabs.html: Flexible or nested data that varies row to row, denormalized read-heavy workloads, or rapid prototyping. Easy to start; you trade some query power, joins, and consistency guarantees. MongoDB, Firestore.

tabs.label: In practice
tabs.html: Real systems often pair a relational core with a cache (Redis) or search index. Don't agonize early — a relational database rarely becomes the thing you regret.

blocks.label: Normalization prevents update anomalies
blocks.html: If you stored the customer's email on every booking row, changing an email means updating dozens of rows — and missing one leaves inconsistent data (an update anomaly). Normalization keeps each fact in one place (email lives on customers) and links with a foreign key. Document stores often denormalize deliberately for read speed, accepting that trade-off.

blocks.q: A foreign key is a column that…
options: References another table's primary key, enforcing a relationship
blocks.explain: A foreign key stores a reference to another table's primary key (each booking's customer_id points to a customers.id), which both models the relationship and lets the database enforce referential integrity.

lessons.title: SQL you will actually write — and indexes
glossary: Read rows, optionally filtered by a condition.
Combine rows from related tables on a matching key.
Collapse rows into groups and compute COUNT/SUM/AVG per group.
A sorted data structure (usually a B-tree) enabling O(log n) lookups on a column instead of an O(n) full scan.
The database's chosen strategy for a query, viewable with EXPLAIN.

blocks.html: You don't need to be a DBA, but reading and writing everyday SQL is a core skill. Four statement shapes cover the vast majority of real work.

blocks.code:
-- read with a filter
SELECT id, name FROM customers WHERE email = 'ada@x.com';

-- add a row, returning what was created
INSERT INTO bookings (customer_id, starts_at)
VALUES (1, '2026-08-01 18:00') RETURNING *;

-- combine related tables
SELECT c.name, b.starts_at
FROM bookings b
JOIN customers c ON c.id = b.customer_id
WHERE b.starts_at > NOW();

-- aggregate per group
SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM bookings
GROUP BY customer_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 3;

blocks.html: The single biggest performance lever is the index. Without one, WHERE email = ? scans every row — O(n). With a B-tree index on email, the database binary-searches to the row in O(log n). This is the same complexity story from the JavaScript module, now at the data layer.

blocks.label: Never build SQL by string concatenation
blocks.html: Writing "...WHERE email = '" + input + "'" invites SQL injection: an input like ' OR '1'='1 rewrites your query. Always use parameterized queries with placeholders ($1, ?) so the driver sends data separately from code. This one habit closes one of the oldest, most damaging vulnerabilities.

blocks.label: Indexes aren't free
blocks.html: Every index speeds reads but slows writes (the index must be updated) and uses storage. Index the columns you filter, join, and sort on — not every column. Use EXPLAIN to confirm the database actually uses an index rather than guessing.

blocks.q: Adding a B-tree index on a frequently filtered column changes lookups from…
options: O(n) full scan to O(log n) search
It has no effect on lookups
blocks.explain: Without an index the database scans every row (O(n)); a B-tree index lets it binary-search to matching rows in O(log n). The trade-off is slower writes and extra storage, so index selectively.

blocks.q: The safe way to include user input in a query is…
blocks.explain: Parameterized queries keep data separate from SQL code, so injected SQL is treated as a literal value and can't execute. It's the definitive defense against SQL injection.

lessons.title: Connecting an app: pools, ORMs, migrations & transactions
glossary: A reusable set of open DB connections, avoiding the cost of connecting per request.
Object-Relational Mapper — query the DB via code objects/methods instead of raw SQL (Prisma, Sequelize).
A versioned, code-tracked change to the schema, applied reproducibly across environments.
A group of statements that commit together or roll back together (all-or-nothing).
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the guarantees a relational transaction provides.

blocks.html: Your API talks to the database over a pooled connection. You can write raw SQL or use an ORM for convenience and type-safety. Either way, the endpoint from the backend module now persists for real — with parameterized queries and error handling.

When several statements must succeed or fail together, wrap them in a transaction. The canonical example is a transfer: debit one account, credit another. If the credit fails after the debit, money vanishes — unless both are in one atomic transaction that rolls back on error.

blocks.label: Migrations keep every environment in sync
blocks.html: A migration is a versioned script that evolves the schema (add a column, a table, an index). Tracking migrations in code means your laptop, staging, and production can all reach the identical schema reproducibly — and roll back if needed. It's how real teams change a live database without chaos or 'works on my machine.'

blocks.q: Why wrap a debit-then-credit money transfer in a single transaction?
options: So both statements commit together or roll back together, preventing money from being lost mid-way
blocks.explain: Transactions give atomicity (the A in ACID): if the second update fails, the first is rolled back, so you never end up with money debited but not credited. Anything that must be all-or-nothing belongs in one transaction.

blocks.q: An ORM primarily lets you…
options: Query the DB through code objects/methods instead of hand-writing SQL
blocks.explain: An Object-Relational Mapper maps tables to objects/methods so you work in your language, often adding type-safety and integrated migrations. You can still drop to raw SQL when needed.

questions.q: A safe default database for structured, related app data is…
options: A relational database such as Postgres
questions.explain: Relational databases handle typed, related, consistent data with powerful queries and transactions — the default for most business apps.

questions.q: A primary key…
questions.explain: The primary key uniquely identifies rows; foreign keys reference it to form relationships.

questions.q: To combine rows from related tables you use…
questions.explain: JOIN merges rows across tables on a matching key (e.g. bookings.customer_id = customers.id).

questions.q: An index on a filtered column changes a lookup from…
options: O(n) scan to O(log n) search
questions.explain: A B-tree index lets the database binary-search instead of scanning every row — at the cost of slower writes and extra storage.

questions.q: SQL injection is prevented by…
questions.explain: Parameters send data separately from SQL code, so malicious input is treated as a literal value, not executable SQL.

questions.q: A transaction guarantees that a group of statements…
options: Commit together or roll back together (atomicity)
questions.explain: Transactions provide all-or-nothing atomicity (the A in ACID), essential for operations like transfers that must not partially complete.

questions.q: A migration is…
options: A versioned, code-tracked schema change applied reproducibly across environments
questions.explain: Migrations version schema changes so development, staging, and production converge on the same schema and can roll back safely.

Tests several units together (e.g. a route plus its database).

blocks.label: Test behavior and edge cases, not implementation
blocks.html: Good tests assert what a function returns for meaningful inputs — including empty, zero, negative, and boundary cases — not how it computes internally. Tests coupled to internals break on every refactor and stop protecting you; tests coupled to behavior survive refactors and catch real regressions.

blocks.title: Two habits of a well-tested codebase

cards.label: Pure where possible
cards.html: Functions with no side effects (same input → same output) are the easiest to test. Push side effects (I/O, DOM) to the edges and keep the core pure.

cards.label: Mock the boundaries
cards.html: Stub the network and the clock so tests are fast and deterministic. A test that hits a real API is slow, flaky, and fails when you're offline.

blocks.q: According to the testing pyramid, you should have…
options: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few E2E tests
blocks.explain: The pyramid puts many cheap, fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, and a thin layer of slow, brittle E2E tests. Inverting it (the 'ice-cream cone') makes the suite slow and flaky.

blocks.q: Why mock the network in a unit test?
options: To keep the test fast, deterministic, and independent of being online
Because mocking is required by JavaScript
blocks.explain: Mocking the boundary removes slowness and flakiness and lets the test run offline with predictable inputs, so it exercises your logic rather than a third party's uptime.

lessons.title: Integrating AI (LLM APIs)
glossary: Large Language Model — the AI you call via an API (Claude, GPT).
The instruction and context you send the model.
A chunk of text the model bills and reasons in; cost and limits scale with tokens.
Retrieval-Augmented Generation — fetch relevant data, put it in the prompt, then ask.
A confident but fabricated model output; mitigated by grounding and validation.
Receiving the response incrementally for a responsive UI.

blocks.html: Adding AI is, mechanically, just another API call — made from your server so the key stays secret (the security lesson applies directly). You send messages, you get text back. The engineering is in the guardrails, not the call.

blocks.title: RAG in four steps ('a chatbot that knows our docs')
steps: Index
Split the client's documents into chunks and store vector embeddings.
Retrieve
For a question, find the most semantically relevant chunks.
Augment
Insert those chunks into the prompt as grounding context.
Generate
Ask the model to answer using only that context — grounded, not guessed.

blocks.label: Cost, trust & guardrails
blocks.html: LLM calls bill per token and can be confidently wrong (hallucinate). Cap max_tokens, bound and validate user input, cache repeats, and never let the model take irreversible actions (payments, deletes, emails) without a human or a validation gate. Treat model output as an untrusted suggestion, not a command.

blocks.q: Why call the LLM from your server rather than directly from the browser?
options: To keep the API key secret and add guardrails (limits, validation, logging)
blocks.explain: Frontend code is public, so a key there would be stolen and drained. Calling from the server keeps the secret safe and gives you a place to cap tokens, validate input/output, cache, and log.

blocks.q: RAG improves answer accuracy by…
options: Retrieving relevant data and feeding it into the prompt as grounding context
blocks.explain: RAG grounds the model in retrieved, relevant source material so it answers from your data rather than from parametric memory alone, reducing hallucination.
