lessons.title: Deployment, environments & CI/CD
glossary: Putting your app on infrastructure the public can reach.
A named context (development, staging, production) with its own config and data.
Continuous Integration/Delivery — automatically test and deploy on every push.
Serves frontend files from edge locations worldwide (Netlify, Vercel, Pages).
Bundling/transpiling source into optimized, fingerprinted assets to serve.
Reverting to a previous known-good deploy when something breaks.

blocks.html: "It works on my machine" is not shipped. Deployment puts your static frontend on a CDN, your backend on a server or serverless platform, and your database on a managed host — each reading configuration from environment variables, per environment.

blocks.label: Three environments prevent disasters
blocks.html: Keep development (your laptop), staging (a production-like rehearsal), and production (real users) separate, each with its own database and keys. You validate risky changes in staging so a bad deploy never touches real customer data. This discipline is a large part of what clients are really paying a professional for.

blocks.code:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml — run tests on every push, deploy on main
name: CI
on: [push]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20 }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test          # fail the build if tests fail
      # deploy step runs only on main, after tests pass

blocks.label: A deploy you can't undo is a liability
blocks.html: Always have a rollback path — most platforms keep previous deploys one click away — and gate deploys behind passing tests in CI. The goal is that shipping is boring: automated, reversible, and low-drama, so you deploy often and small rather than rarely and huge.

blocks.q: Why keep staging and production as separate environments?
options: To validate changes in a production-like setting before real users and real data are exposed to risk
blocks.explain: Staging is a safe rehearsal with its own database and keys, so you can catch breakage before it reaches customers. Mixing them means every experiment risks real user data.

blocks.q: The main purpose of CI running your test suite on every push is…
options: To catch regressions automatically before code is merged or deployed
blocks.explain: Continuous Integration runs the tests on every change so failures surface immediately, keeping the main branch deployable and making shipping safe and routine.

modules.title: Capstone: Ship a Full-Stack Feature
modules.tagline: Design, build, secure, test, and deploy a real booking feature end to end — then defend it in review.
objectives: Translate a written brief into a data model, API contract, and UI.
Implement a full CRUD slice across frontend, API, and database with real error handling and security.
Add automated tests and deploy to a live environment with separate config.
Justify your engineering decisions the way you would in a code review or to a client.

lessons.title: The brief & how to approach it
glossary: The agreed request/response shape of each endpoint — the interface between frontend and backend.
One feature built through every layer (UI → API → DB) rather than one layer built fully.
The explicit checklist a feature must meet before it's considered complete.
A peer reading your change and asking why — the forcing function for defensible decisions.

blocks.html: This capstone ties every module together. You'll build a small but complete vertical slice: a class-booking feature for a fictional studio, spanning the database, a REST API, and an accessible frontend — deployed and tested. The goal isn't size; it's that every layer is done properly and you can explain why.

The scenario. "Studio 7" runs classes. Customers should be able to view available class times, book a spot with their name and email, and see their bookings. Staff must not be able to double-book a full class. The studio owner wants it live, on their own hosting, maintainable by whoever they hire next.

blocks.title: A professional approach, in order
steps: Model the data
Design tables: classes (id, title, starts_at, capacity) and bookings (id, class_id FK, name, email, created_at). Decide constraints and indexes.
Define the API contract
GET /classes, GET /classes/:id/bookings, POST /classes/:id/bookings (201 or 409 when full). Write the request/response shapes before coding.
Build the slice
Implement the endpoints with parameterized queries and validation, then the frontend that consumes them with proper loading/error states.
Secure it
Validate on the server, escape output, parameterize queries, keep secrets in env, set sensible status codes.
Test & deploy
Unit-test the capacity logic, integration-test the POST route, then deploy frontend + API + DB across environments with CI.

blocks.label: Write the contract first
blocks.html: Deciding the exact request and response JSON — and the status codes, including the 409 Conflict when a class is full — before you write code forces the hard questions early and lets the frontend and backend be built in parallel against the same agreement. This is how real teams work.

blocks.q: Why decide the API contract (paths, request/response shapes, status codes) before writing code?
options: It surfaces hard questions early and lets frontend and backend be built in parallel against one agreement
blocks.explain: A contract-first approach forces decisions like 'what happens when a class is full?' (a 409) up front, documents the interface, and decouples the two sides so they can progress independently and integrate cleanly.

blocks.html: Now the frontend consumes the API. The pattern from the DOM and async modules applies directly: keep state, render from state, and — critically for a real product — show honest loading and error states rather than a blank screen or a silent failure.

blocks.label: Loading and error states are not optional polish
blocks.html: A screen that shows nothing during a slow network, or silently does nothing on failure, reads as broken to users. The three states — loading, success, error — are part of the feature's definition of done, not a nicety. This is a frequent gap between a demo and a shippable product.

blocks.q: Why build the class list with createElement + textContent instead of innerHTML with the class titles?
options: textContent prevents any HTML in the data from executing (XSS) while innerHTML would run it
blocks.explain: Class titles ultimately come from data that may include user or admin input; textContent renders them as literal text, closing the XSS hole that innerHTML would open. It's the same output-safety rule from the DOM and security modules.

lessons.title: Build, test, ship — and defend it
glossary: A bug where concurrent requests interleave to produce an invalid state (e.g. two bookings exceeding capacity).
Making a repeated request safe — relevant if a user double-submits the booking form.
The explicit criteria your finished work is evaluated against.

blocks.html: Below is the capacity check at the heart of the feature. Note the subtlety: checking the count and then inserting in two separate steps is a race condition — two simultaneous requests can both pass the check and overfill the class. The professional fix is to enforce it in one atomic step (a transaction with a constraint, or a conditional insert), exactly the transaction reasoning from the database module.

blocks.label: The check-then-act trap
blocks.html: A tempting first draft reads the count, compares in JavaScript, then inserts. Between the read and the insert, another request can slip in — both see space, both insert, capacity is exceeded. Any "check then act" on shared state needs a transaction or a database constraint to be correct under concurrency. This is the kind of bug a code reviewer will look for.

blocks.title: Assignment: Ship the Studio 7 booking feature
blocks.brief: Build and deploy the full vertical slice described in this module: a database schema for classes and bookings, a REST API (list classes, list a class's bookings, create a booking with a capacity check), and an accessible frontend that lists classes and lets a user book one. Deploy it live with separate configuration, and write a short README explaining your decisions. Then be ready to defend every choice as if in a code review.
items: A strong result models data correctly: a bookings.class_id foreign key, sensible types/constraints, and an index on the column you filter/join on.
A strong result uses correct HTTP semantics: GET to read, POST to create, 201 on success with a Location, 400 on invalid input, 409 when the class is full, 404 for a missing class.
A strong result enforces capacity atomically (transaction or conditional insert), demonstrably free of the check-then-act race condition.
A strong result is secure: parameterized queries throughout, server-side validation, output escaped in the UI (no innerHTML with user data), and all secrets in environment variables.
A strong result is accessible: labeled form controls, keyboard-operable, visible focus, and AA-contrast text.
A strong result handles async honestly: loading and error states in the UI, res.ok checked, and failures surfaced to the user rather than swallowed.
A strong result includes automated tests: at least a unit test of the capacity rule and an integration test of the create-booking route (including the 409 path).
A strong result is deployed and reproducible: frontend on a static host/CDN, API and database hosted, config per environment, and a README that justifies the key engineering decisions.

blocks.q: Reading a class's booking count, comparing it in JavaScript, then inserting the booking is unsafe because…
options: Two concurrent requests can both pass the check before either inserts, overfilling the class (a race condition)
blocks.explain: Between the read and the insert, another request can interleave; both see available space and both insert, exceeding capacity. Enforce the limit atomically with a transaction or a single conditional insert so the check and the act cannot be split.

questions.q: When a client POSTs a booking to a class that is already full, the most correct status code is…
questions.explain: 409 Conflict signals that the request conflicts with the current state of the resource (no capacity). 201 would falsely claim success; 500 wrongly blames the server for a valid, expected domain condition.

questions.q: Enforcing class capacity by counting in JavaScript and then inserting risks…
options: A race condition under concurrent requests
questions.explain: Check-then-act on shared state lets concurrent requests both pass the check and insert, exceeding capacity. Use a transaction or conditional insert to make it atomic.

questions.q: In the capstone, secrets like the database URL should live…
options: In server-side environment variables, never committed
questions.explain: Frontend code is public; connection strings and keys belong in server environment variables, kept out of the repo and the client.

questions.q: Designing the API contract before coding primarily helps by…
options: Surfacing edge cases early and letting frontend and backend proceed in parallel
